Cloudflare says it is the starting point of the vulnerability harness they now run across their whole fleet.

I measured it before reading it closely. The skill is 15 markdown files: 1,778 lines, 24,768 words, about 183 KB. At the usual four bytes per token that is roughly 46,000 tokens of instructions, loaded in pieces as a run needs them. Cloudflare's blog post says the first version was about 450 lines.

Two zero-dependency Node scripts sit beside the prose: validate-findings.cjs (773 lines) and validate-coverage-ledger.cjs (872 lines). Their own test suites ran clean on my machine, 34 and 31 tests.

The part that caught my eye is the proportion. Of the six phases, two exist only to disprove: Phase 3 hands every candidate to a fresh agent told to refute it, and Phase 5 sends another fresh agent over the final record (the quick profile merges the two). Each Phase 3 verifier prompt carries about 17.5 KB of fixed text before it sees the candidate: a six-step refutation prompt, a file-promotion procedure, and three schema branches copied in verbatim.

What I actually did

I did not install the skill, and no agent ran it. The README's install path is a skills CLI that writes into your agent's config, and I don't do that for a post.

Instead I wrote a small target, played the hunter by hand, and ran the skill's real validator on the result. The target is a notes service on node:http and node:sqlite with dummy users alice and bob. These are the two functions that matter:

function search(user, q) {
  const sql = "SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE owner = '" + user + "' AND title LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
  return db.prepare(sql).all();
}

function getNote(user, id) {
  return db.prepare('SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?').get(id, user);
}

There is also an /admin/export route gated on X-Forwarded-For starting with 10..

Then I wrote four findings the way a hunter returns them, in the skill's schema:

  1. SQL injection in search. Real.
  2. SQL injection in getNote, marked confirmed, with an observed result claiming it returned bob's note. False.
  3. SQL injection in findUser at src/users.js line 212. Invented: that file does not exist.
  4. The export gate trusts a header a client can set, unless a proxy rewrites it. A real question, but the proxy is not in the repo.

What the validator checks 

$ node validate-findings.cjs proposed.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

To be fair to it, it does enforce the contract. When I raised one record's overall severity above its impact, or put a severity on the needs_validation record, it failed, with exact paths. It checks shape, ordering, safe relative paths, and that a confirmed record has an observed result written in visible text.

It never opens a source file. It doesn't take the target path at all. The skill says this itself, in one line of Phase 4: validator success "proves format and ledger consistency only." A hunter's observed result is a string, and my invented one was schema-valid.

A cheap check gets one

Next I wrote 15 lines of Node that open every cited file and check the line exists:

ok   admin/export-xff-gate
ok   notes/note-sql-concat
ok   notes/search-sql-concat
FAIL users/find-user-template-sql  src/routes/login.js: no such file; src/users.js: no such file

That kills the invented file. Cloudflare's harness has the same idea in plain code: per the blog, deterministic code confirms the cited files and paths exist before a finding moves on.

It does nothing for the getNote claim. Line 24 is real, and it really runs a query with the id in it. Every fact the record cites is true except the one that matters.

The skeptic gets the rest

So I walked the Phase 3 prompt by hand. Step 2 says to rebuild the strongest control on the path. For getNote that takes one read: id and owner are bound as placeholders. Step 3 says to reproduce the minimum result yourself. My service is my own code with dummy data, so I ran it on loopback (the skill demands an OS-enforced sandbox before it runs anyone else's target; this was not that). Output trimmed:

search, normal     200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"}]
search, payload    200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"},{"id":2,"title":"payroll"}]
note, bob id       200 null
note, payload      200 null
note, payload 2    200 null
export, XFF 10.    200 [... both users' notes ...]

The search payload ' OR 1=1 -- hands alice the title of bob's note. Every getNote payload returns nothing. The export gate opens to a header alone, but whether a client can send that header in production depends on a proxy the repo doesn't contain, so it stays needs_validation with an owner check attached. That is the skill's rule for a deployment fact, and I agree with it.

The final file: one confirmed, one needs validation, two rejected.

$ node validate-findings.cjs findings.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

Same validator, same four fingerprints, same PASS. In between, two of the three "confirmed" bugs became rejected. Only reading the code at the cited line and running the payload told the files apart.

Why the skeptic is the expensive part

Finding candidates is cheap now. Cloudflare's blog reports 20,799 raw candidates from their discovery harness, of which about 12,057 survived validation, and an early validation rejection rate of 40% before better recon brought it down to 11%. At 40%, a team without a refuter gets four bad tickets in every ten. Somebody pays for those, and it's usually a maintainer.

That is also the theme of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" post on coordinating disclosure as agents surface critical bugs, which was on the Hacker News front page the same day.

So my claim: when you judge an AI security tool, judge the step that tries to prove the finding wrong. The hunt is a hypothesis generator. The product is the record that survived.

Where it falls short

Cost is real. In the Hacker News thread, jesse_dot_id reported at least 150k tokens on a fairly small FastAPI project before hitting a session limit. Issue #20 is a blind test on one seeded target, three rounds per arm, by a team with its own competing tool, which it discloses. There the quick profile cost a median $29.95 against $2.06 for one plain agent, and found the same share of the seeded bugs (a median recall of 0.467 for both). On a small, clean target the skeptic may have nothing to kill.

And a skeptic that shares the hunter's model is not fully independent. Per that same issue, the skill's verifiers inherit the session's model. Cloudflare's own pipeline triages with a different model from the one that hunts. Fresh context is not a different mind.

If you run AI reviews on your code today, what does the step that tries to disprove a finding look like: a second model, a test that must fail before the fix, or you?

articles.title: I Got Tired of Switching Tools While Coding on My Phone, So I Built This
articles.description: Hey everyone!  I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the things I'm most proud of is its built-in Developer Panel.

The reason I wanted this is pretty simple: I develop stuff on my phone. 💀

When you're developing a website, you need to check logs, investigate requests, see what's happening on the server, and figure out why something isn't working. Switching between tools just to do that gets annoying pretty quickly on a phone.

So I wanted those tools available right inside the framework I'm already using.

That's where the Developer Panel comes in.

What is Authtics Host?

Authtics Host is a web framework inspired by Next.js. It uses TypeScript, TSX, React, and Esbuild, and supports SSR (Server-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), CSR (Client-Side Rendering), and SRTWS (Site Rendering Through WebSockets, which is currently in beta).

I'm still working on improving it, but I wanted to share one of its features that has genuinely helped me while developing.

Getting started

First, you'll need Node.js 22.

Install Authtics Host using npm:

npm install @bananacool467/authtics-host@latest

For a basic project, you can use a structure like this:

my-project/
├── index.ts
├── authtics_host.config.ts
└── client/
    └── pages/
        └── index.tsx

In index.ts, create the app:

import { App } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

const app = new App();

Then configure the framework in authtics_host.config.ts:

import { defineConfig } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  autoFile: true,
  autoPage: true,
  autoPageDir: "client/pages",
  autoFileDir: "client/public"
});

Finally, create client/pages/index.tsx:

export default function Index() {
  return (
    <p>Hello, World!</p>
  );
}

Start the project with:

node --experimental-strip-types index.ts

You should get your page, and with development mode enabled, you should also see a clickable Developer Panel at the bottom-right.

So, what's in the Developer Panel?

The panel has eight tabs:

  • Console — View current logs.
  • Route — Check information about the current route.
  • Webpage Info — See information about the current webpage.
  • Network — Check the current ping and inspect fetch requests sent from the client and responses received from the server.
  • Client Info — View the client's user agent, operating system, and FPS.
  • About Host — Check the current Authtics Host version.
  • Server Info — Check server heap usage, CPU usage, request count, connected users, and uptime.
  • Panel Customization — Customize the Developer Panel.

Here's what it looks like:


The panel gives you somewhere to look when you're trying to figure out what's going on with your application, without having to keep switching to a separate tool for every little thing.

For example, if a request isn't behaving the way you expected, you can check the Network tab. If you're trying to figure out what the application is logging, you can check the Console tab.

You also have route and client information available when you need it.

Obviously, this doesn't mean you will never need other debugging tools. It's just convenient to have these features available in the framework itself.

It can do more than inspect things

The Developer Panel also has controls for managing the running app.

Depending on how you've configured access, you can restart or shut down the app and pause or resume incoming users.

That can be useful when you're testing something and need to control what's happening without going off to manage the server separately.

A quick note about developer access

The panel uses something called a DAT (Developer Access Token).

If you configure a DAT in authtics_host.config.ts, you can restrict developer access using a token you specify:

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  dat: "YOUR DAT HERE"
});

Replace YOUR DAT HERE with your own token. Don't publish a real token in your source code or share it publicly.

You can also configure an array of DATs if multiple developers need access.

Without a DAT restriction configured, the panel only provides access to the Console and Network tabs. Setting a DAT restriction enables access to the other developer features, including the app management controls.

Since the panel can expose information about your app and provide controls over the server, make sure you configure access appropriately before deploying anything publicly. You can also turn the panel off by setting devMode to false.

Why I built it this way

This is the part that matters most to me.

I didn't build the Developer Panel just to have another feature to list in a README. I built it because I actually use it.

When you're coding on a phone, little inconveniences add up. Having the console, network information, client details, and server information in one place means I don't have to keep interrupting my workflow to go somewhere else just to investigate what's happening.

And that's really the goal of Authtics Host: make web development more convenient, especially for people working from mobile devices.

I'm not saying this will magically make every developer faster, or that everyone needs another framework. I built something that solves a problem I personally ran into, and the Developer Panel has helped me with my own work.

That's a pretty good reason for me to keep improving it.

Try it out

Authtics Host is available on npm:

https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bananacool467/authtics-host

The package includes more than just the Developer Panel, so check out the README for the other framework features and configuration options.

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to hear what works for you and what needs improvement. Feedback is useful, especially while the project is still evolving.

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: You should use Map instead of object literals for lookup tables
articles.description: A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still...
articles.body_html:
A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still think the idea behind it is a good one: map an input to an output, skip the long list of case and break, and keep your code short and readable.

But there's a catch I didn't cover back then, and a reader (thanks Dario!) pointed it out in the comments: plain objects don't only contain the keys you put in them.

So in this article I want to show you what the problem is, and why today I'd reach for a Map instead.

A quick recap

In the previous article we had something like this:

const getAnimalSound = animal => {
  const sounds = {
    dog: 'woof',
    cat: 'meow',
    cow: 'moo',
    default: 'unknown sound',
  };

  return sounds[animal] || sounds.default;
};

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));   // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger')); // 'unknown sound'

Clean, short, and it works. Or at least it looks like it does.

So what's the problem?

Every object you create with {} inherits from Object.prototype. This means that when you read sounds[animal], if JavaScript doesn't find the key on the object itself, it goes up the prototype chain and looks there too.

And Object.prototype has quite a few properties on it, like constructor, toString, valueOf, hasOwnProperty and __proto__.

Let's see what happens if we pass one of those names to our function:

console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // [Function: Object]
console.log(getAnimalSound('toString'));    // [Function: toString]
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // [Object: null prototype] {}

None of those return 'unknown sound'. Because the value we get back is truthy, the || sounds.default fallback never kicks in, and we return something completely unexpected.

Now, you might think "who would ever pass constructor as an animal?". And you are probably right, until that value comes from a query string, a form field, or the body of an API request. Then anybody can pass whatever they want.

It gets worse with functions

In the previous article we also used object literals to dispatch commands:

const executeCommand = command => {
  const commands = {
    greet: () => console.log('Hello there!'),
    farewell: () => console.log('Goodbye!'),
    default: () => console.log('Unknown command'),
  };

  (commands[command] || commands.default)();
};

Let's try a few "commands":

executeCommand('constructor');    // nothing happens, it silently calls Object()
executeCommand('toString');       // nothing happens either
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object

The first two fail silently, which is the worst kind of bug, because you don't even know something went wrong. The last one crashes your function.

And with nested objects

The state machine example is my favourite one:

const stateTransitions = {
  idle: { start: 'loading' },
  loading: { success: 'loaded', error: 'error' },
};

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions[currentState]?.[action] || currentState;

console.log(handleStateTransition('constructor', 'name')); // 'Object'
console.log(handleStateTransition('idle', 'toString'));    // [Function: toString]

Yes, your component is now in the 'Object' state, or worse, its state is a function.

Note
To be clear, this is not prototype pollution. Prototype pollution happens when an attacker manages to write to Object.prototype, for example with obj[key] = value where key is __proto__. Here we are only reading, but it's still a real bug, and it's the reason why security linters like eslint-plugin-security flag obj[variable] lookups.

Enter Map

A Map is a built-in collection of key/value pairs, and the important difference is that map.get(key) only returns entries that you explicitly added. There's no prototype chain to walk through, so constructor is just a key like any other, and since you never added it, you get undefined.

Let's rewrite our first example:

const sounds = new Map([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = animal => sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound';

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));         // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger'));       // 'unknown sound'
console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // 'unknown sound' ✅
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // 'unknown sound' ✅

You might have noticed a few other small changes, and they are not random:

  • The Map is defined outside the function, so we don't rebuild it every time the function is called.
  • The fallback is no longer stored as a default key, so nobody can "select" it by passing 'default'.
  • I'm using ?? (nullish coalescing) instead of ||. With ||, a valid value like 0 or an empty string would be replaced by the fallback. With ??, the fallback is used only when the value is null or undefined.

Tip
If you already have an object and you don't want to rewrite it as an array of arrays, you can convert it with new Map(Object.entries(myObject)).

Dispatching functions

The same works for our commands:

const commands = new Map([
  ['greet', () => console.log('Hello there!')],
  ['farewell', () => console.log('Goodbye!')],
  ['time', () => console.log(`Current time: ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`)],
]);

const unknownCommand = () => console.log('Unknown command');

const executeCommand = command => (commands.get(command) ?? unknownCommand)();

executeCommand('greet');          // 'Hello there!'
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // 'Unknown command' ✅

And with parameters, like the calculator from the previous article:

const operations = new Map([
  ['add', (x, y) => x + y],
  ['subtract', (x, y) => x - y],
  ['multiply', (x, y) => x * y],
  ['divide', (x, y) => (y !== 0 ? x / y : 'Cannot divide by zero')],
]);

const calculator = (a, b, operation) => {
  const fn = operations.get(operation);
  return fn ? fn(a, b) : 'Unknown operation';
};

console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'add'));     // 8
console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'valueOf')); // 'Unknown operation' ✅

The state machine

For nested lookups you can nest Maps too:

const stateTransitions = new Map([
  ['idle', new Map([['start', 'loading'], ['reset', 'idle']])],
  ['loading', new Map([['success', 'loaded'], ['error', 'error'], ['cancel', 'idle']])],
  ['loaded', new Map([['refresh', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
  ['error', new Map([['retry', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
]);

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions.get(currentState)?.get(action) ?? currentState;

let state = 'idle';
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'start');    // 'loading'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'success');  // 'loaded'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'toString'); // 'loaded' (unchanged) ✅

I'll be honest, this one is a bit less pretty than the object version. We'll come back to that in a moment.

A bonus with TypeScript

If you use TypeScript, Map has another nice side effect: map.get() always returns T | undefined, so the compiler forces you to handle the missing case.

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = new Map<Animal, string>([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = (animal: Animal): string =>
  sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound'; // without ?? TypeScript will complain

When you don't need a Map

As always, I don't want you to take this as "never use objects again". There are cases where a plain object is perfectly fine.

When the keys never come from outside your code. If the key is a value you control, for example a TypeScript literal union that you pass around internally, the prototype issue can't really happen. In that case an object with satisfies gives you great type checking:

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = {
  dog: 'woof',
  cat: 'meow',
  cow: 'moo',
} satisfies Record<Animal, string>;

Just remember that TypeScript types disappear at runtime: if the value comes from a request or a form, you still need to validate it.

When you only need a quick safety check. If you want to keep the object syntax, Object.hasOwn() checks only the object's own properties, ignoring the prototype chain:

const getAnimalSound = animal =>
  Object.hasOwn(sounds, animal) ? sounds[animal] : 'unknown sound';

This is also a good option for deeply nested tables like the state machine, where nested Maps get a bit noisy.

When you need to serialise the data. JSON.stringify(new Map([['a', 1]])) returns {}, not what you expect. If your lookup table needs to be sent over the wire or saved as JSON, an object is easier to work with.

When switch is simply the better tool. As I mentioned in the previous article, if your conditions involve ranges, complex expressions or intentional fall-through, a switch is still the right choice.

Conclusions

Object literals are still a great idea to replace long switch statements, but when the key comes from user input, a plain object can return things you never put in it, like constructor or toString.

A Map fixes that by design: it only knows the keys you gave it, it works nicely with ??, and with TypeScript it forces you to handle the missing case.

So my rule of thumb today is simple:

  • If the key comes from outside your code, use a Map.
  • If the key is fully under your control, an object is fine, and Object.hasOwn() is a cheap safety net if you want one.

I hope this helped you to understand the hidden gotcha of object lookups, and as always any comments are welcome!

Disclaimer

Parts of this article were created with the help of AI.

articles.title: I Didn’t Want AI to Build My App. I Wanted to Learn How to Build It Myself.
articles.description: I was in Class 7 when I first properly touched a computer. My first lesson was simple: how to turn it...
articles.body_html:
I was in Class 7 when I first properly touched a computer. My first lesson was simple: how to turn it on and how to turn it off.

After that, the computer was handed over to me.

My friend Tahir Bilal had almost the same experience. We had a teacher, and we still respect that teacher for introducing us to the computer. But what happened afterwards was something neither of us had planned. From the very next day, we started teaching other students what we had learned.

We were not experts. We barely knew the basics. Yet, somehow, we had started teaching ourselves and others without anyone formally teaching us how to learn.

Looking back, I think that was the beginning of something that would take more than a decade to find its direction.

What made us self-learners was not a sophisticated computer laboratory, an expensive course, or access to professional trainers. It was curiosity. We wanted to know what else a computer could do, and every little discovery made us want to explore further.

We waited years for that curiosity to find the right opportunity.

When the ambition was bigger than the resources

By Class 10, I had started imagining that I could write code and build applications of my own. The problem was that there were no accessible coding courses around us, and the Chenab Valley offered very few opportunities for someone with that kind of ambition.

If you lived in a major city, you might have found an institute, a mentor, or someone who could introduce you to programming. For us, the internet was the classroom, and even that classroom was painfully slow.

We were using 2G internet. YouTube was not the learning platform it would later become for millions of people. Finding a useful tutorial, opening a webpage, and understanding a piece of code could take considerable patience.

Around 2009, I began experimenting with websites on Wapka.mobi, a mobile website-building platform that gave beginners like me an opportunity to work with HTML. It allowed me to create websites, experiment with layouts, and gradually understand how the web worked.

I was convinced I was coding.

Then I came across JavaScript tutorials.

Suddenly, what I thought I understood seemed much more complicated. Looking at the code made my head ache. I wondered how anyone could learn to write something that complicated. I had the desire, but I lacked the guidance to cross that gap.

This is an important distinction that people often overlook when discussing talent. A person can have the curiosity and determination to learn something but still struggle because the right resources, explanations, and support are missing.

I did not stop because I had lost interest. I simply did not know how to proceed.

When Wapka eventually shut down its services around 2014–2015, I moved towards Blogger, Google's blogging platform. By then, journalism and activism had also begun to occupy an important place in my life.

In 2014, while I was in Class 11, I was writing press releases about protests we organised over basic public demands, including roads and school buses. Our concerns were local, but we understood that documenting them and communicating them to the outside world mattered.

My journey into journalism and local activism is discussed in my booklet Power of Local Journalism. But the desire to build things independently never disappeared. I wanted my own website, my own platform, and eventually my own applications.

The illusion of being a developer

For years, I tried different platforms that promised to turn ideas into mobile applications without requiring much programming knowledge.

At one point, I got access to a friend's Google Play Console account and uploaded an application I had created using AppsGeyser. I thought I had become an app developer.

Within months, the app or its publishing arrangement was blocked. I never established whether the problem was related to the platform, my application, or something else. What I learned was that creating an application through a website and understanding how an application is built are two different things.

I also tried Android Studio. Repeatedly.

Each attempt ended in frustration. I could not understand the code well enough to make meaningful progress. I would start learning, get stuck, and eventually move on to something else. GitHub confused me, too. I could see that developers were using it, but I could not understand what purpose it served or how it fitted into the process of building software.

I asked friends to develop applications for me. Some agreed, but their commitments and professional lives meant they could not always find the time. That was understandable. They had their own responsibilities, and I could not expect them to put their lives on hold for my ideas.

Hiring a professional developer was not a realistic option either. I did not have the budget.

Meanwhile, the ideas kept accumulating.

I had learned enough about the internet to imagine what I wanted to build, but not enough to build it independently. For years, that gap between imagination and execution remained one of my biggest frustrations.

The turning point came when I stopped waiting

In 2025, some friends introduced me to PowerShell and GitHub and demonstrated some basic operations. I began experimenting with them myself. I used these tools for drafting Right to Information applications and other practical work before gradually moving towards software development.

One decision proved particularly important: I asked a friend who had begun working on an application for The Chenab Times to send me the project files so I could continue the work myself.

My friend Farhat Usman, who is exceptionally capable with technology, had also faced resource constraints. He did not have consistent access to a stable laptop or PC. That made it difficult for him to work continuously on the project.

Another friend, Mohsin Hassan, who is currently at Jammu University, discussed various tools and possibilities with me.

Eventually, I reached a point where I had to make a choice. I could keep waiting for someone to build my ideas, or I could take responsibility for learning how to build them.

There is a saying in our local language that captures this perfectly:

Yo'tam Na Paan Ka'rekh, To'tam Bani Na Ke'in.

In Hindi, the meaning is straightforward: Jab tak khud nahi karoge, tab tak kuch nahi banne wala.

Until you try to do it yourself, nothing is going to happen.

I began coding through PowerShell, working with the project files, and using ChatGPT as a guide. The experience was far from smooth. Early AI-generated code often contained errors, and I did not always know how to identify or correct them.

There were times when a suggested solution introduced another problem. A feature that seemed simple in conversation could become complicated when I tried to implement it in an actual project.

But this time, I had something I had not possessed during my earlier attempts: a way to ask questions continuously, examine alternatives, and work through problems one at a time.

I also had years of experience with website development, prompting, and experimenting with digital tools. Some programming concepts were not entirely unfamiliar to me. I had encountered C++ basics, and Dart and Flutter gradually became more understandable as I worked with them.

I was no longer trying to learn everything before building anything. I was learning by building, and the project itself was becoming my classroom.

AI did not replace my learning. It made learning possible.

I use ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Replit, and other AI-powered tools. But there is a significant difference between how I approached them and how people sometimes assume AI-assisted development works.

I did not simply ask an AI to build my application and accept whatever it produced.

I wanted to understand how to do things myself.

I would ask how a particular feature worked, where a change needed to be made, why an error was appearing, or how one part of the application communicated with another. For a single feature in The Chenab Times application, discussions could continue for hours.

Sometimes the AI's explanation was wrong. Sometimes its proposed code did not fit the existing project. Sometimes a fix worked in one place but broke something elsewhere. I had to learn to question the answers rather than treat them as instructions that could never fail.

That is one of the most important lessons I have learned from AI-assisted development: the ability to generate code is not the same as the ability to build reliable software.

An application is not just a collection of screens. Its components must work together. Authentication must be handled correctly. Data must be stored and retrieved reliably. Errors must be investigated. Existing features must continue to work after new ones are introduced.

As my projects grew, I realised that I needed to understand not only how to write or modify code but also how to test applications, inspect project structures, work with databases, use version control, review changes, and investigate failures.

GitHub, which once seemed incomprehensible, gradually became a practical part of my workflow. Branches, commits, migrations, testing, and reviewing changes became things I could discuss and work with rather than mysterious terminology.

I also learned that AI tools can confidently suggest the wrong solution. A developer who blindly copies their output is vulnerable to mistakes. A learner who asks why the solution should work, tests it, and investigates when it fails has an opportunity to develop genuine technical judgment.

AI did not remove the need to learn. It gave me a way to keep learning when a human teacher was not available.

Two months, one application, and years of preparation

My determination was particularly evident when I developed ScanPatra V1 in approximately two months.

ScanPatra is a document productivity application built with Flutter. It brings document scanning, OCR, PDF creation, and related utilities into a single workflow, with an emphasis on offline use and local document handling.

Developing it was not simply a matter of generating a few screens. It involved bringing multiple features together, testing how they behaved, identifying problems, and working through technical limitations.

There were difficult moments, but the experience changed how I viewed my own capabilities. Something I had imagined for years was finally becoming a real product that other people could install and use.

ScanPatra eventually reached the Google Play Store. Another application also made it to the store, while Journoist remains under development as I continue building and refining its features.

These are not just three separate projects. They represent different stages of the same journey: from experimenting with simple websites, to struggling with Android Studio, to taking responsibility for real applications.

My work can also be explored through my personal website, "AnzerAyoob.com".

The most important change was not that I suddenly became capable of writing perfect code. I did not. It was that I stopped treating my lack of formal training as a permanent barrier.

Journoist: building for a purpose

Journoist is particularly important to me because it brings my experience in journalism and activism into software development.

The application is intended to provide tools for journalists and activists, including verification and research features and a civic campaign system. Its planned features include campaigns, petitions, and a social publishing format called Drops.

Building such a platform presents challenges that go beyond the visible interface. A campaign system needs appropriate data structures, moderation workflows, and reliable handling of signatures. A social publishing feature needs its own rules for visibility, links, interactions, and moderation. Accounts, permissions, and user roles must behave consistently.

These are the kinds of problems that force a learner to go beyond superficial coding.

I have had to work with Flutter and Dart on the application side, PHP and MariaDB on the backend, Firebase authentication, database migrations, and GitHub-based development workflows. I have also learned the importance of protecting existing functionality while introducing new features.

Journoist is still a work in progress, and I do not consider it finished simply because parts of it run on a phone. A functioning prototype and a dependable public application are not the same thing. It still needs careful testing, security reviews, and continued refinement.

That distinction matters. AI can accelerate development, but it cannot make the responsibility for a product disappear. If people depend on an application, its creator must take its reliability, privacy, and security seriously.

The digital divide is also a learning divide

My experience has made me question the way we discuss technological opportunity in places such as the Chenab Valley.

We often speak about the digital divide as a problem of internet connectivity. Connectivity matters, but the divide goes deeper.

It includes the absence of mentors, affordable training, reliable devices, practical learning environments, and opportunities to experiment without fear of failure. It also includes the difficulty of finding someone who can explain a technical concept in a way a beginner can understand.

For years, I had internet access of a kind, but that did not mean I had meaningful access to programming education.

Artificial intelligence can help reduce some of these barriers. Someone who cannot afford a private coding tutor can now ask questions, request explanations, compare approaches, and receive guidance while working on a real project.

But we should not exaggerate what this means. AI does not provide everyone with a computer, reliable electricity, affordable internet, or the time to learn. Nor does it guarantee that the answers are correct. People still need foundational knowledge, critical thinking, patience, and opportunities to practise.

The promise lies in making technical guidance more accessible, not in pretending that every barrier has disappeared.

Our educational institutions should take this opportunity seriously. Students should not be taught merely to use AI to complete assignments. They should learn to use it to understand difficult concepts, build projects, question answers, test hypotheses, and solve real problems.

A student in a remote village should have a genuine opportunity to learn software development even if there is no coding institute nearby.

That should not be an extraordinary privilege.

The real question is what we do with the tools

There is a growing argument that AI will make programming knowledge unnecessary because anyone can describe an idea and obtain an application.

I disagree with that conclusion.

AI may make some aspects of development easier, but building a useful, secure, maintainable application requires much more than describing an idea. Someone must understand the problem, make architectural decisions, assess the generated code, test the result, and take responsibility when something fails.

At the same time, I reject the opposite argument that AI-assisted development is not real development.

If someone uses AI to learn a programming language, understand an unfamiliar codebase, implement features, debug errors, test changes, and gradually become more capable, dismissing that work merely because AI was involved makes little sense.

The relevant question is not whether every line was typed without assistance. It is whether the person understands the system well enough to make informed decisions and is willing to take responsibility for the outcome.

My own experience is proof that the process can be imperfect and still productive. I began with HTML, struggled with JavaScript, failed to understand Android Studio, became confused by GitHub, and spent years waiting for the right circumstances. Eventually, I found tools that allowed me to continue learning through practical work.

I am still learning. I expect to make mistakes, encounter problems I cannot immediately solve, and discover gaps in my knowledge. That is part of software development, not evidence that the journey has failed.

From a computer in Class 7 to building my own applications

When I think about that first computer in Class 7, I remember how little I knew. I could turn it on and off. Yet that small introduction opened a door that I kept trying to walk through for years.

Tahir Bilal and I began teaching other students the very next day. We did not know where that spirit would lead us. We had no elaborate plan, no roadmap, and no idea how much the technology around us would change.

In the years that followed, I moved between websites, journalism, activism, failed attempts at app development, and long periods of frustration. I did not follow a conventional route into software engineering. I had no formal coding education that could take me from beginner to professional developer in a structured sequence.

What I had was a persistent desire to build something of my own.

Today, AI tools have become guides in a journey that began long before they existed. They have helped me turn curiosity into practical skills and ideas into working applications. But they did not create the curiosity, and they cannot replace the judgment I must continue to develop.

My journey also carries a lesson for anyone who believes that a lack of formal opportunities automatically disqualifies them from learning something difficult. The barriers are real, and determination alone does not solve every problem. Yet the absence of a perfect environment does not mean there is nothing you can do.

Start with what is available. Build something small. Ask questions. Read the code. Test it. Break things. Fix them. Learn enough to recognise when a tool is giving you a bad answer. Then move on to something more ambitious.

Do not spend your entire life waiting for somebody else to build what you have imagined.

I once thought that coding was beyond my reach because I could not understand JavaScript tutorials. Years later, I was working on applications involving mobile interfaces, databases, authentication, and backend systems. The distance between those two points was covered by years of curiosity, repeated failures, self-learning, and eventually the assistance of AI.

I did not need AI to give me a dream. I already had one.

I needed the opportunity to learn how to pursue it.

And that, perhaps, is the greatest promise of these tools: not that they will build everything for us, but that they may help more of us learn to build things for ourselves.

articles.title: Can AI Crawlers See Your JavaScript? A 10-Minute curl Test for the HTML Bots Actually Get
articles.description: Your page looks perfect in Chrome. Headline, pricing, FAQ, a nice comparison table. But an AI crawler...
articles.body_html:
Your page looks perfect in Chrome. Headline, pricing, FAQ, a nice comparison table. But an AI crawler doesn't open Chrome. It sends one HTTP request, gets back whatever your server returns, and moves on.

If your important text only appears after JavaScript runs, there's a real chance that crawler saw an empty shell. This post shows how to check that in about ten minutes with curl and a couple of one-liners.

Why this matters for AI search

There are two versions of every page:

  1. The initial HTML - what the server sends in response to a request.
  2. The rendered page - what you see after scripts run, APIs return data and widgets load.

Google documents a separate rendering stage for JavaScript (JavaScript SEO basics). Other clients don't have to copy Google's capabilities. In December 2024, Vercel and MERJ published an analysis of AI crawler traffic on Vercel's network (The rise of the AI crawler). They found that OpenAI's crawlers, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and several others fetched JavaScript files but didn't execute them, while Gemini (via Google's infrastructure) and Applebot did render pages. Crawler behavior can change over time, so treat this as a reason to test, not as a permanent rule.

The safe assumption: if a fact isn't in the initial HTML, don't count on an AI crawler seeing it.

Step 1: Pick three pages, not your whole site

Don't start with a full crawl. Choose:

  • a service or pricing page,
  • one article or guide,
  • one product or listing page.

For each one, write down 3-5 facts that must be visible: the H1, the main description, a price or condition, a key claim, and the important internal links.

Step 2: Fetch the raw HTML 

URL="https://example.com/pricing"

curl -sL "$URL" -o raw.html
wc -c raw.html

Ignore the file size. A 300 KB response can be all navigation and inline JSON; a 20 KB response can contain the full answer. What matters is meaning.

To see the response a specific crawler would get, you can also send its user agent string (useful when a CDN or WAF treats bots differently):

curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0 AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko; compatible; GPTBot/1.1; +https://openai.com/gptbot)" \
  -o raw_gptbot.html -w "%{http_code}\n" "$URL"

If this returns 403, 429 or a challenge page while a normal request returns 200, you have a different problem: your firewall, not your rendering. Fix that first.

Step 3: Search for your must-have facts 

for phrase in "Pricing" "per month" "Free trial" "How it works"; do
  if grep -qi "$phrase" raw.html; then
    echo "FOUND:   $phrase"
  else
    echo "MISSING: $phrase"
  fi
done

A match isn't the whole story. Text sitting inside a JSON blob in a <script> tag (for example __NEXT_DATA__ or a hydration payload) is technically "in the HTML," but a normal content extractor may not treat it as the main content. (The Vercel study notes that models can sometimes interpret JSON in the initial response, but you shouldn't rely on it.) Check where the match lives:

grep -o -i ".\{80\}per month.\{80\}" raw.html | head

If every hit is inside a script, mark it as "present in data, not in markup."

Step 4: Strip the markup and read it like a bot

A quick way to see the visible text without a browser:

python3 - <<'PY'
import re, html
t = open("raw.html", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").read()
t = re.sub(r"(?is)<(script|style|noscript|svg)[^>]*>.*?</\1>", " ", t)
t = re.sub(r"(?s)<[^>]+>", " ", t)
t = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(t)).strip()
print(len(t.split()), "words")
print(t[:1500])
PY

Read the first 1,500 characters. Does it say what the page is about and what you offer? Or is it "Loading... Menu Sign in Cookie settings"?

Step 5: Compare with the rendered page

Open the same URL in your browser, open DevTools and compare the rendered DOM with raw.html. Note which important elements only exist after load: tabs, accordions filled by API calls, pricing tables from a widget, reviews from a third-party script.

Also test direct URL access. Single-page apps sometimes work when you click from the homepage but return a generic shell (or a 404) when the route is requested directly. Crawlers always request directly.

Step 6: Fix delivery, not the content

If the useful text is missing from the initial HTML, the usual options are:

  • Server-side rendering (SSR) for pages that change often.
  • Static generation / prerendering for pages that change rarely.
  • Moving critical facts into the server-rendered template (H1, intro, price, key FAQ answers) while keeping interactive extras client-side.

Don't build a separate "bot version" with different claims. Visitors and crawlers should get the same meaning; serving different content to bots is the kind of thing that backfires.

Step 7: Save before and after

When the fix ships, re-run the same curl and the same checks. Keep both files:

curl -sL "$URL" -o "after_$(date +%F).html"

A fix is done when the main text is present in a direct request, the page still works for humans, and the required links are there. That removes a technical barrier. It doesn't make the page relevant to every question or guarantee a citation, so track discovery and citations separately.

A quick checklist

  • [ ] Three representative pages chosen
  • [ ] Must-have facts listed per page
  • [ ] Raw HTML fetched (normal UA and crawler UA)
  • [ ] Status codes match between the two
  • [ ] Facts found in markup, not only in script data
  • [ ] Direct URL access tested for app routes
  • [ ] Fix verified with a before/after snapshot

If you want this check done automatically, AURA GEO audits the HTML your server actually returns, flags pages where little readable text comes through, and turns that into tasks you can hand to your own agent over MCP. There's a longer explainer here: how to tell whether a crawler can see the text on a JavaScript website.

articles.title: On-Device AI in React Native with Expo: Local LLM, Speech-to-Text, Vision & Fully Local Agents
articles.description: There are billions of phones out there that can already run AI models locally, but most apps don't...
articles.body_html:
There are billions of phones out there that can already run AI models locally, but most apps don't use that at all. Sending every AI request to a server is wasteful, especially for simple ones, and there are a lot of those. It costs money, it adds latency and the user's data leaves their phone. At scale it also adds up in the energy and water data centers use. I think it's important that we start making use of what these devices can already do. expo-ai-kit is my small contribution to that.

It's an Expo module for running AI on the device. This post shows how to use it for text generation, speech-to-text and vision in an Expo/React Native app. Everything runs locally on the phone, using the models and frameworks that iOS and Android already ship with (Apple Foundation Models, Apple Speech and Vision, ML Kit on Android).

saidkaban / expo-ai-kit

On-device AI for Expo and React Native. Local LLM, speech-to-text, vision, and embeddings. No API keys, no cloud.

expo-ai-kit

On-device AI for React Native. Local LLM, speech-to-text, vision, and embeddings for Expo apps and React Native apps with Expo modules installed. No API keys, no cloud.

Documentation · Examples · npm · Changelog

  • Private and offline. Inference runs on the device. Prompts, audio, and images never leave it.
  • No API key, no per-request cost. Nothing to provision, meter, or proxy.
  • One TypeScript API for both platforms. Apple Foundation Models, Speech, and Vision on iOS ML Kit and MediaPipe on Android; LiteRT-LM for downloadable models such as Gemma, Qwen, and Phi.
  • Pay only for what you use. Every feature is opt-in, so unused native code, models, and permissions never ship. Zero runtime JavaScript dependencies.

Install

npx expo install expo-ai-kit

Turn on the features you use in your app config, then make a native build. Until you enable a feature, none of its native code is compiled into your app…

View on GitHub

Setup 

npx expo install expo-ai-kit

Features are off by default. You enable the ones you need in app.json, and only those get compiled into your app:

{
  "expo": {
    "plugins": [
      ["expo-ai-kit", { "llm": true, "speech": true, "vision": true }]
    ]
  }
}

You need Expo SDK 54+ and a development build. Expo Go won't work since this is native code.

On-device LLM

On iOS 26+ this uses Apple Foundation Models (Apple Intelligence devices). On Android it uses the ML Kit Prompt API on supported devices.

import { isAvailable, prepareBuiltInModel, sendMessage } from 'expo-ai-kit';

if (await isAvailable()) {
  await prepareBuiltInModel();

  const { text } = await sendMessage([
    { role: 'user', content: 'Explain gravity in one sentence.' },
  ]);
}

prepareBuiltInModel() matters on Android because the model may need to download the first time.

Streaming:

import { streamMessage } from 'expo-ai-kit';

const { promise, stop } = streamMessage(
  [{ role: 'user', content: 'Write a very short story.' }],
  (event) => setText(event.accumulatedText)
);

const { text } = await promise;

The calls are stateless, so you send the whole message history each time. You're not limited to the built-in models either. You can download capable models like Gemma 4 and run them on both iOS and Android with setModel(). There's also generateObject for JSON output, generateText for tool calling and a Vercel AI SDK provider under expo-ai-kit/ai.

Speech-to-text

iOS 26+ uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer, Android 12+ uses ML Kit speech recognition.

import {
  getSpeechRecognitionAvailability,
  prepareSpeechRecognition,
  requestSpeechPermissionsAsync,
  streamTranscription,
} from 'expo-ai-kit';

const availability = await getSpeechRecognitionAvailability({ locale: 'en-US' });
if (availability.status === 'downloadable') {
  await prepareSpeechRecognition({ locale: 'en-US' });
}

const permission = await requestSpeechPermissionsAsync();
if (!permission.granted) return;

const { promise, stop } = streamTranscription(
  (update) => setTranscript(update.text),
  { locale: 'en-US' }
);

// later
stop();
const { text } = await promise;

For recorded audio files there's transcribe({ audio: { uri } }). On iOS it also returns timestamps. On Android, files are processed at real-time speed, so it's better for short voice notes than long recordings.

Vision

iOS uses the Vision framework and needs no config. Android uses ML Kit.

OCR:

import { recognizeText } from 'expo-ai-kit';

const result = await recognizeText({ uri: photo.uri });
console.log(result.text);

Image labels:

import { labelImage } from 'expo-ai-kit';

const labels = await labelImage({ uri: photo.uri }, { maxResults: 5 });
// [{ label: 'Dog', confidence: 0.97 }, ...]

Background removal:

import { removeBackground } from 'expo-ai-kit';

const cutout = await removeBackground({ uri: photo.uri });
// cutout.uri is a PNG with a transparent background

URIs from expo-image-picker or expo-camera work directly. There's also detectFaces for face bounding boxes.

Combining speech and the LLM

Speech and text generation don't block each other, so you can transcribe and then send the result to the model:

const { promise, stop } = streamTranscription((u) => setTranscript(u.text));

// when the user is done talking
stop();
const { text: question } = await promise;

const { text: answer } = await sendMessage([
  { role: 'system', content: 'Keep answers short.' },
  { role: 'user', content: question },
]);

Some limitations

  • Not every device supports every feature. Check availability before calling and have a fallback.
  • Some vision features don't work in the iOS simulator, so test on a real device.
  • Only one LLM generation can run at a time. A second call throws INFERENCE_BUSY.
  • These are small models. They work well for things like summarizing, extracting info and short replies, less so for long or complex tasks.

Where this is going

The part I'm most excited about is on-device agents. Most of the pieces are already in the library. The model can call your functions with generateText, it can hear the user with speech-to-text and it can see with vision. Put those together and you get an agent that lives on the phone and does things for the user, like setting a reminder or finding a photo, without a single request going to a server.

Small models aren't great at long multi-step tasks yet, but they're getting better fast. That's the direction I'm taking expo-ai-kit.

Links

  • Docs: https://expo-ai-kit.dev
  • GitHub: https://github.com/saidkaban/expo-ai-kit
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/expo-ai-kit

If you try it, I'd like to hear how it goes. Issues and PRs are welcome. A star on GitHub also helps the vision I mentioned at the beginning.

articles.title: DORA for Financial-Sector Suppliers: Essential Preparations for ICT Providers
articles.description: Understand the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and prep your ICT services for compliance in the financial sector.
articles.body_html:
Introduction

The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is a significant legislative measure aimed at ensuring that the financial sector is resilient against IT disruptions. As a financial-sector supplier, particularly those providing Information and Communication Technology (ICT) services, understanding DORA's implications and preparing accordingly is crucial. This article outlines necessary actions for ICT providers under DORA to ensure compliance and foster resilience in their services.

What is DORA?

DORA aims to strengthen the IT resilience of the European financial space. It is designed to address challenges posed by increasing digitalization in the sector, ensuring a comprehensive approach to operational resilience. Its requirements cover various aspects, including risk management, testing, and reporting, effectively shaping the regulatory landscape in which ICT suppliers operate.

Understanding DORA’s Core Requirements

DORA introduces several key regulations that ICT providers must adhere to:

1. Risk Management Frameworks

Providers need to develop comprehensive risk management frameworks that identify, assess, and manage ICT risks effectively. This involves:

  • Conducting regular risk assessments.
  • Establishing governance structures that include accountability for digital resilience.
  • Defining risk appetite and tolerance levels.

2. Incident Reporting

ICT providers must implement effective incident detection and reporting mechanisms. The requirements include:

  • The establishment of protocols for detection, management, and reporting of ICT-related incidents.
  • Timely notification of incidents to relevant authorities and stakeholders, ideally within 24 hours.

3. Testing and Validation of Resilience

DORA mandates that ICT suppliers perform regular testing of their operational resilience. Recommended practices include:

  • Conducting stress tests and scenario analyses to assess the robustness of systems.
  • Implementing a framework for coordination with financial institutions during testing phases to ensure alignment and understanding.

4. Third-party Risk Management

ICT suppliers must also have strategies in place to manage third-party risks. This involves:

  • Due diligence assessments of vendors to evaluate their operational resilience.
  • Continuous monitoring of third-party risks throughout the relationship.

Steps to Prepare for DORA Compliance

Preparing for DORA compliance entails several action steps that ICT providers must undertake:

1. Conduct a Gap Assessment

Start with a comprehensive gap assessment to understand your current standing in relation to DORA requirements. Identify areas where your processes and controls may fall short. This assessment should ideally include:

  • A review of existing policies and procedures.
  • Identification of compliance gaps, including both technical and procedural weaknesses.

2. Enhance Your Risk Management Framework

Based on findings from the gap assessment, enhance your risk management framework to meet DORA’s expectations. Focus on:

  • Integrating IT risk management with overall business risk management.
  • Documenting processes clearly and establishing accountability for risk management tasks.

3. Develop Incident Management Protocols

Establish incident management protocols that align with DORA’s requirements. Ensure that your protocols include:

  • Clear definitions of what constitutes an incident.
  • Procedures for timely communication and escalation within the organization.

4. Implement Continuous Monitoring Practices

DORA requires that ICT providers have mechanisms in place for continuous monitoring of their ICT systems. This may include:

  • Deployment of automated monitoring tools to detect anomalies.
  • Regular audits and reviews to assess the effectiveness of existing controls and processes.

Cross-Framework Mapping

Understanding how DORA aligns with other regulatory frameworks is essential for ICT suppliers working in multiple jurisdictions. Cross-framework mapping can help:

  • Identify overlapping requirements between DORA, ISO 27001, SOC 2, and other standards, enabling organizations to streamline their compliance efforts.
  • Reduce redundancy and overlap in efforts to establish a cohesive compliance strategy.

Security Testing for Compliance

Regular security testing is vital for demonstrating compliance with DORA. Consider the following:

  • Engage in penetration testing programs to simulate real-world attacks and evaluate system vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly conduct vulnerability assessments to identify and remediate security weaknesses in a timely manner.

Evidence and Audit Preparation

Preparing for potential audits requires documenting compliance efforts thoroughly. Key activities include:

  • Collecting evidence that demonstrates adherence to DORA requirements.
  • Maintaining an organized record of policies, risk assessments, incident reports, and security testing outcomes.

The Role of Bitkosh Technologies

While this article has focused on the necessary preparations for ICT providers under DORA, organizations may benefit from professional guidance. Bitkosh Technologies specializes in compliance readiness and can assist in gap assessments, cross-framework mappings, and evidence preparation. Such support can enhance your operational processes and increase the likelihood of a successful audit.

Conclusion

As the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) comes into effect, ICT providers serving the financial sector must take proactive steps to prepare. Understanding its core requirements and implementing the necessary framework adjustments are crucial for compliance and operational resilience. By engaging in proactive risk management, effective incident response planning, and targeted security testing, ICT providers can not only comply with DORA but also contribute to a more resilient financial ecosystem.
